claim: Chronologically aging yeast cells undergo a sudden redox collapse that affects over 80% of identified thiol-containing proteins.
source: Here, we report the discovery that chronologically aging yeast cells undergo a sudden redox collapse, which affects over 80% of identified thiol-containing proteins.
evidence: The manuscript presents OxICAT mass spectrometry data showing widespread protein thiol oxidation during chronological aging, as shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: The redox collapse in aging yeast is not triggered by an increase in endogenous oxidants.
source: We present evidence that this redox collapse is not triggered by an increase in endogenous oxidants as would have been postulated by the free radical theory of aging.
evidence: The manuscript provides evidence that peroxide-sensitive proteins like GapDH are not among early oxidation targets, and that only 5 of 28 early oxidation targets were previously identified as peroxide-sensitive.

claim: The redox collapse appears to be instigated by a substantial drop in cellular NADPH.
source: Instead it appears to be instigated by a substantial drop in cellular NADPH, which normally provides the electron source for maintaining cellular redox homeostasis.
evidence: The manuscript presents NADPH measurements (Figure 6B) showing decreased levels that correlate temporally with protein oxidation events.

claim: The decrease in NADPH levels occurs very early during lifespan and sets into motion a cascade that is predicted to down-regulate most cellular processes.
source: This decrease in NADPH levels occurs very early during lifespan and sets into motion a cascade that is predicted to down-regulate most cellular processes.
evidence: The manuscript shows NADPH decrease occurs within 24 hours after exponential growth (Figure 6B) and precedes widespread protein oxidation affecting metabolic enzymes, translation machinery, and other cellular processes.

claim: Caloric restriction increases NADPH levels and delays each facet of the cascade.
source: Caloric restriction, a near-universal lifespan extending measure, increases NADPH levels and delays each facet of the cascade.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that caloric restriction delays NADPH decrease by 48 hours (Figure 6B), delays protein oxidation (Figure 2A), and extends lifespan (Figure 1A).

claim: The redox collapse occurs days before cell death.
source: Our studies reveal a time line of events leading up to the system-wide oxidation of the proteome days before cell death.
evidence: The manuscript shows that protein oxidation occurs at day 3 under standard conditions while mean lifespan is ~7 days (Figure 1A, Figure 2A).

claim: The free radical theory of aging postulates that aging is caused by an accumulation of oxidative damage to cellular macromolecules.
source: One leading hypothesis is the free radical theory of aging, which postulates that aging is caused by an accumulation of oxidative damage to cellular macromolecules (Harman, 1956).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harman, 1956.

claim: Many lines of correlative evidence support the free radical theory of aging.
source: Many lines of correlative evidence support this theory (Muller et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Muller et al., 2007.

claim: Recent studies in mice have generated conflicting results as few genetic manipulations targeting conserved antioxidant genes showed the predicted effects on lifespan.
source: However, while these studies confirm the general notion that oxidative damage is associated with aging, recent studies in mice have generated conflicting results as few of the genetic manipulations targeting conserved antioxidant genes showed the predicted effects on lifespan (Perez et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perez et al., 2009.

claim: It is unclear whether oxidative damage is a cause of aging or simply a consequence.
source: Hence, the jury is still out on the question of whether oxidative damage is a cause of aging or simply a consequence (Salmon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Salmon et al., 2010 and represents a summary of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Protein carbonylation is the most commonly used read-out for oxidative protein damage.
source: So far, the most commonly used read-out for oxidative protein damage involves detection of protein carbonylation (Shacter et al., 1994; Levine, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shacter et al., 1994 and Levine, 2002.

claim: Neither the extent of carbonylation nor the specific effect(s) of carbonylation on protein activity are easily assessed.
source: However, neither the extent of carbonylation nor the specific effect(s) of carbonylation on protein activity are easily assessed.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of protein carbonylation as a measurement technique, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: OxICAT is a highly sensitive and fully quantitative mass spectrometry-based redox technique that allows determination of the in vivo oxidation status of hundreds of different protein thiols.
source: To get a better handle on evaluating oxidative protein modifications, we developed a highly sensitive and fully quantitative mass spectrometry-based redox technique (i.e., OxICAT) that allows us to determine the in vivo oxidation status of hundreds of different protein thiols in organisms and to identify the proteins affected (Leichert et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leichert et al., 2008 and describes the method used in the current study.

claim: OxICAT was used to quantify the steady-state oxidation status of almost 400 different yeast protein thiols and identify proteins that contain peroxide and redox-sensitive cysteines.
source: We recently used OxICAT in Saccharomyces cerevisiae to quantify the steady-state oxidation status of almost 400 different yeast protein thiols and identify those proteins that contain peroxide and redox-sensitive cysteines (Brandes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brandes et al., 2011, which describes previous work by the authors.

claim: The chronological lifespan of S. cerevisiae represents a popular model system for analyzing aging in postmitotic cells.
source: The chronological lifespan of S. cerevisiae represents a popular model system for analyzing aging in postmitotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the use of yeast as a model system, supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Chronological lifespan is defined as the length of time that non-dividing cells remain viable in a high metabolic state.
source: Chronological lifespan is defined as the length of time that non-dividing cells remain viable in a high metabolic state (Fabrizio and Longo, 2007; Fontana et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fabrizio and Longo, 2007 and Fontana et al., 2010.

claim: Chronological lifespan decreases in yeast strains lacking the oxidant scavenging enzymes superoxide dismutase (SOD) or catalase.
source: In support of the free radical theory of aging, chronological lifespan decreases in yeast strains lacking the oxidant scavenging enzymes superoxide dismutase (SOD) or catalase (Longo et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Longo et al., 1996.

claim: Chronological lifespan increases when glutathione or SOD levels are elevated.
source: chronological lifespan decreases in yeast strains lacking the oxidant scavenging enzymes superoxide dismutase (SOD) or catalase (Longo et al., 1996) and increases when glutathione or SOD levels are elevated (Harris et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2003.

claim: Caloric restriction significantly increases chronological lifespan in yeast.
source: Also, caloric restriction, a nearly universal measure to extend lifespan, has been shown to significantly increase chronological lifespan in yeast (Fontana et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fontana et al., 2010.

claim: One unifying trait among calorically restricted organisms is a significantly increased oxidative stress resistance.
source: Although the molecular mechanism by which caloric restriction extends lifespan has not been elucidated, one unifying trait among calorically restricted organisms is a significantly increased oxidative stress resistance (Barja, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barja, 2002.

claim: Under standard conditions (2% glucose SCD media), DB746 cells maintain their high metabolic, postdiauxic state until they die with a mean lifespan of approximately 7 days.
source: Under standard conditions, 2% glucose SCD media is used and DB746 cells maintain their high metabolic, postdiauxic state until they die (mean lifespan ∼7 days) (Fabrizio and Longo, 2007) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fabrizio and Longo, 2007 and by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Under caloric restriction (0.5% glucose SCD media), yeast cells show increased respiration, higher oxidative stress resistance, and extended lifespan with a mean lifespan of approximately 11 days.
source: Under caloric restriction (CR), 0.5% glucose SCD media is used, which increases respiration, promotes higher oxidative stress resistance, and extends lifespan (mean lifespan ∼11 days) (Figure 1A) (Fabrizio and Longo, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fabrizio and Longo, 2003 and by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: With the starvation diet (2% glucose for 2 days followed by water), yeast cells switch to a hypometabolic state and show dramatically increased lifespan with a mean lifespan greater than 15 days.
source: With the starvation diet, cells are provided 2% glucose SCD media for 2 days followed by incubation in water. Under these conditions, yeast cells switch to a hypometabolic state (stationary phase) and show dramatically increased lifespan (mean lifespan > 15 days) (Figure 1A) (Fabrizio et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fabrizio et al., 2003 and by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GapDH has some of the most redox-sensitive cysteines in yeast and other organisms.
source: To initially determine whether and when ROS levels change during yeast chronological aging, we analyzed the thiol oxidation status of glyceraldehyde-3-P dehydrogenase (GapDH, TDH) as this protein has some of the most redox-sensitive cysteines in yeast and other organisms (Brandes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brandes et al., 2011.

claim: GapDH contains two redox-sensitive cysteines (the active site Cys150 and the nearby Cys154), and both are found in the same tryptic peptide (GapDH144–160).
source: GapDH contains two redox-sensitive cysteines (the active site Cys150 and the nearby Cys154), and both of these are found in the same tryptic peptide (GapDH144–160).
evidence: This is a statement about the structure of GapDH based on previous characterization.

claim: The two redox-sensitive cysteines in GapDH form an intramolecular disulfide bond during peroxide stress in vivo.
source: We previously suggested that these cysteines form an intramolecular disulfide bond during peroxide stress in vivo (Brandes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brandes et al., 2011.

claim: During the first 2 days of cultivation under either standard or caloric restriction conditions, less than 30% of the two cysteines in GapDH144–160 were oxidized.
source: During the first 2 days of cultivation under either standard or caloric restriction conditions, we found that the GapDH144–160 peptide was predominantly labeled with two light ICAT molecule and less than 30% of the two cysteines were calculated to be oxidized (Figures 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: Within 24 hours after day 2 (i.e., day 3) of cultivation under standard conditions, about 70% of the GapDH peptide was oxidized.
source: However, within the next 24 hr (i.e., day 3) of cultivation under standard conditions, about 70% of the GapDH peptide was labeled with two heavy ICAT molecules, indicating that both cysteines were oxidized (Figure 1C, compare red and blue trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The extent of GapDH oxidation at day 3 under standard conditions is very similar to that observed in yeast cells treated with 0.5 mM H2O2 for 15 min.
source: This extent of oxidation is very similar to that observed in yeast cells treated with 0.5 mM H2O2 for 15 min (Brandes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brandes et al., 2011.

claim: On day 4 under standard conditions, over 80% of all GapDH molecules were oxidized.
source: On day 4 under standard conditions, over 80% of all GapDH molecules were oxidized, indicating that by that time, glycolysis is dramatically reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by OxICAT data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The oxidation status of GapDH from yeast cells cultivated under caloric restriction conditions remained low for the first 4 days of cultivation.
source: In contrast, the oxidation status of GapDH from yeast cells cultivated under caloric restriction conditions remained low for the first 4 days of cultivation (Figures 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1B and 1D.

claim: Under caloric restriction conditions, significant GapDH oxidation occurred within a 24-hour time window, with over 70% of all GapDH molecules affected by day 5 and almost 90% affected by day 7.
source: Then, however, significant oxidation occurred (also within a 24-hr time window), with over 70% of all GapDH molecules affected by day 5 and almost 90% affected by day 7 (Figure 1D, purple trace and black trace, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Yeast cells cultivated in standard media for 2 days and then switched into water showed no significant increase in GapDH oxidation over the monitored time span.
source: Yeast cells cultivated in standard media for 2 days and then switched into water showed no significant increase in GapDH oxidation over the time span that was monitored by OxICAT (Figure 1B, open circles and Figure 1—Source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Under hypometabolic conditions, cells maintain GapDH in its reduced and active state over extended periods of time.
source: suggesting that under hypometabolic conditions, cells maintain GapDH in its reduced and active state over extended periods of time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GapDH oxidation does not increase significantly when cells are shifted to water.

claim: 286 protein thiols were reproducibly identified in all samples taken under standard 2% glucose conditions (all four replicates at five different time points).
source: We reproducibly identified 286 of these protein thiols in all samples taken under standard 2% glucose conditions (i.e., all four replicates at five different time points) (Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: 263 protein thiols were identified in the four replicates and seven time points taken from cultures cultivated under caloric restriction conditions.
source: Most of these protein thiols were also identified in the four replicates and seven time points taken from cultures cultivated under caloric restriction conditions (i.e., 263 peptides)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: 100 protein thiols were reproducibly identified under hypometabolic water starvation conditions.
source: and 100 of these peptides were reproducibly identified under hypometabolic water starvation conditions as well (Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: The majority of identified protein thiols followed an oxidation pattern similar to that of GapDH's active site cysteines.
source: We discovered that the majority of our identified protein thiols found in standard and caloric restriction conditions followed an oxidation pattern similar to that of GapDH's active site cysteines (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Protein thiols were largely reduced for the first 48 hr post log phase under standard conditions or for the first 96 hr post log phase under caloric restriction conditions, and then became suddenly oxidized within a 24-hr period.
source: The protein thiols were largely reduced (Figure 2A, blue) for the first 48 hr post log phase (i.e., day 0) under standard conditions or for the first 96 hr post log phase under caloric restriction conditions, and then became suddenly oxidized within a 24-hr period (Figure 2A, red).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After one more day of cultivation, the majority of protein thiols were oxidized to over 80%.
source: After one more day of cultivation, the majority of these protein thiols were then oxidized to over 80% (Figure 2A and Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Shifting cells to water at day 2 of cultivation in 2% glucose SCD media prevented the sudden onset of oxidation, and proteins showed only a minor increase in their thiol oxidation state.
source: Shifting cells to water at day 2 of cultivation in 2% glucose SCD media prevented this sudden onset of oxidation, and proteins showed only a minor increase in their thiol oxidation state, which persisted until at least day 10 (Figure 2A and Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Over 40 oxidation-sensitive proteins play crucial roles in protein translation, including 27 different thiol-containing ribosomal proteins, several translation initiation and elongation factors, translational activators, and numerous tRNA synthetases.
source: For instance, we found over 40 oxidation-sensitive proteins that play crucial roles in protein translation, including 27 different thiol-containing 40S, 60S, and 54S ribosomal proteins, several translation initiation (e.g., TIF11, GCD1) and elongation factors (e.g., EFT2, TEF1, TEF3), translational activators (e.g., GCN1), and numerous tRNA synthetases (e.g., MES1, KRS1, VAS1).
evidence: This claim is based on the identification of these proteins in the OxICAT dataset.

claim: Oxidation of translation-related proteins most likely affects the rate and extent of protein synthesis in chronologically aging yeast cells.
source: Oxidation of these proteins most likely affects the rate and extent of protein synthesis in chronologically aging yeast cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of the oxidized proteins.

claim: Numerous metabolic enzymes including ACO1, PGK1, IDP1, PDC1, and TPI1 become oxidized, likely affecting processes ranging from the Krebs cycle and the pentose phosphate pathway to fatty acid and amino acid synthesis.
source: Moreover, we found countless metabolic enzymes, including ACO1, PGK1, IDP1, PDC1, and TPI1 to become oxidized, likely affecting processes ranging from the Krebs cycle and the pentose phosphate pathway to fatty acid and amino acid synthesis.
evidence: This claim is based on the identification of these proteins in the OxICAT dataset and inference about their functions.

claim: Numerous oxidation-sensitive proteins are involved in maintaining protein homeostasis, including chaperones, prolyl isomerases, components of the proteasome complex, ubiquitination machinery, and cellular antioxidant response proteins.
source: Also, numerous oxidation-sensitive proteins that we identified are known to be involved in maintaining protein homeostasis, including chaperones (e.g., YDJ1, HSP78, SSA1/2, SSB1/2, SSE1/2, SSZ1), prolyl isomerases (e.g., FPR1/2, CPR1, 6), components of the proteasome complex (e.g., PRE10, PUP2), and ubiquitination machinery (e.g., UBC4), or serve as part of the cellular antioxidant response (e.g., PRDX, thioredoxin reductase1/2) (Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the identification of these proteins in the OxICAT dataset shown in Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Many of the identified proteins have previously been found to contain redox-sensitive cysteines.
source: Many of these proteins have previously been found to contain redox-sensitive cysteines (Lindahl et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lindahl et al., 2011.

claim: Over 33% of the 290 different protein thiols monitored have been confirmed to be redox-sensitive in yeast or other organisms.
source: In fact, of the 290 different protein thiols that we monitored in our study, over 33% have been confirmed to be redox-sensitive in yeast or other organisms (Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the RedoxDB database and data shown in Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: An additional 20% of identified cysteines are localized to proteins that have been found to contain redox-sensitive cysteines but whose redox-sensitive cysteines have not yet been fully identified.
source: Moreover, an additional 20% of our identified cysteines are localized to proteins that have been found to contain redox-sensitive cysteines but whose redox-sensitive cysteines have not yet been fully identified.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the RedoxDB database.

claim: The RedoxDB database compiled and manually curated over 2100 proteins with over 2300 redox-sensitive cysteines from different eukaryotic organisms.
source: These percentages were obtained by comparing our list of aging-oxidized protein thiols with the recently published RedoxDB database, which compiled and manually curated over 2100 proteins with over 2300 redox-sensitive cysteines from different eukaryotic organisms (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: Over 80% of an unbiased population of thiol-containing yeast proteins have the capacity to become significantly oxidized under physiologically relevant growth conditions.
source: Our finding that over 80% of an unbiased population of thiol-containing yeast proteins have the capacity to become significantly oxidized under physiologically relevant growth conditions (Figure 1—Source data 1) suggests that reversible cysteine oxidation, such as that detected with our OxICAT method, is a much more widespread event than previously anticipated.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Reversible cysteine oxidation is a much more widespread event than previously anticipated.
source: Our finding that over 80% of an unbiased population of thiol-containing yeast proteins have the capacity to become significantly oxidized under physiologically relevant growth conditions (Figure 1—Source data 1) suggests that reversible cysteine oxidation, such as that detected with our OxICAT method, is a much more widespread event than previously anticipated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 80% of protein thiols become oxidized.

claim: Oxygen consumption measurements indicate that chronologically aging yeast cells are metabolically active in the stationary phase.
source: Despite the limited supply of nutrients in the stationary phase, oxygen consumption measurements indicate that chronologically aging yeast cells are metabolically active in this phase (Fabrizio et al., 2003; Fabrizio and Longo, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fabrizio et al., 2003 and Fabrizio and Longo, 2003.

claim: Intracellular ATP is maintained at levels equivalent to or above those present during exponential growth for up to 5 days under standard postmitotic growth conditions and for at least 7 days under caloric restriction conditions.
source: Consistent with earlier ATP measurements conducted in chronologically aging yeast cells (Goldberg et al., 2009), we found that intracellular ATP is indeed maintained at levels equivalent to or above those present during exponential growth for up to 5 days when cultivated under standard postmitotic growth conditions and for at least 7 days under caloric restriction conditions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 2009 and by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chronologically aging yeast cells are not starving and are able to maintain their energy resources and survive for extended periods of times despite a heavily oxidized proteome.
source: These results demonstrate that chronologically aging yeast cells are not starving and are able to maintain their energy resources and survive for extended periods of times despite (or possibly even because of) a heavily oxidized proteome.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATP measurements and viability data.

claim: Several protein thiols showed oxidation that preceded the global wave of oxidation by 24–48 hr.
source: In addition, however, we noticed several protein thiols whose oxidation appeared to precede this global wave of oxidation by 24–48 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: More than 95% of identified protein thiols clustered into one of seven distinct oxidation clusters (named A–G).
source: More than 95% of our identified protein thiols clustered into one of seven distinct oxidation clusters (named A–G) and most protein thiols maintained their cluster assignment independent of the cultivation condition (standard or caloric restriction media) (Figure 3 and Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Most protein thiols maintained their cluster assignment independent of the cultivation condition (standard or caloric restriction media).
source: More than 95% of our identified protein thiols clustered into one of seven distinct oxidation clusters (named A–G) and most protein thiols maintained their cluster assignment independent of the cultivation condition (standard or caloric restriction media) (Figure 3 and Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Clusters A–C contained the majority of identified peptides and included all those thiol groups that revealed a sudden onset of oxidation by either day 3 in standard media or day 5 in caloric restriction media.
source: Clusters A–C contained the majority of our identified peptides and included all those thiol groups that revealed a sudden onset of oxidation by either day 3 in standard media or day 5 in caloric restriction media.
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: About 10% of identified peptides preceded the general oxidation trend by 24–48 hr (clusters D and E).
source: About 10% of identified peptides preceded this general oxidation trend by 24–48 hr (Figure 3, clusters D and E and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Peptides in clusters D and E showed significantly higher oxidation levels at either day 1 or day 2 compared to their oxidation states at day 0.
source: These peptides showed significantly higher oxidation levels at either day 1 (Figure 3, cluster D) or day 2 (Figure 3, cluster E) compared to their oxidation states at day 0.
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most protein thiols that were subject to early oxidation under one condition were found to be early oxidation targets under the other cultivation condition as well.
source: Importantly, most of these protein thiols that were subject to early oxidation under one condition were found to be early oxidation targets under the other cultivation condition as well.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of cluster assignments across different cultivation conditions.

claim: Early oxidation targets are of particular interest because their oxidation may serve as an early warning of age-induced changes in the oxidative status of cells or might induce changes in their activity that control or trigger the oxidation of proteins in general.
source: These peptides are of particular interest because their oxidation may not just serve as an early warning of age-induced changes in the oxidative status of cells, but might induce changes in their activity, which are involved in controlling or triggering the oxidation of proteins in general.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential significance of early oxidation targets.

claim: About 15% of the identified cysteine-containing yeast peptides remained reduced (cluster F) or stayed oxidized (cluster G) throughout the course of the incubation.
source: Only about 15% of the identified cysteine-containing yeast peptides remained reduced (Figure 3, cluster F) or stayed oxidized (Figure 3, cluster G) throughout the course of the incubation (Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Analysis of the subcellular distribution of proteins in individual clusters did not reveal any significant correlation between the location of the proteins and their oxidation pattern.
source: Analysis of the subcellular distribution of the proteins in the individual clusters did not reveal any significant correlation between the location of the proteins and their oxidation pattern (apart from the expected accumulation of proteins of the endoplasmic reticulum and secreted proteins in cluster G) and reflected well the general subcellular distribution of all identified proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of the identified proteins.

claim: Cysteine thiols that became oxidized early (clusters D and E) as well as protein thiols with high steady-state levels of oxidation during exponential growth (clusters C and G) had a significant accumulation of additional cysteines in close proximity.
source: The most noticeable difference among the thiol groups in the individual clusters was that those cysteine thiols that became oxidized early (clusters D and E) as well as protein thiols with high steady-state levels of oxidation during exponential growth (clusters C and G) had a significant (p<0.05) accumulation of additional cysteines in close proximity (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Protein thiols that stayed reduced (cluster F) or were initially reduced and followed the general oxidation trend (clusters A and B) almost completely lacked the presence of nearby additional cysteines.
source: In contrast, those protein thiols that stayed reduced (cluster F) or were initially reduced and followed the general oxidation trend (clusters A and B) almost completely lacked the presence of nearby additional cysteines.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Chi-square-analysis confirmed the significance of the finding that early-oxidized cysteines have nearby additional cysteines and excluded the dominance of any other amino acid type apart from cysteine in close vicinity of the identified thiol.
source: Chi-square-analysis confirmed the significance of this finding and excluded the dominance of any other amino acid type apart from cysteine in close vicinity of the identified thiol (Table 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis shown in Table 2A and 2B.

claim: The early oxidation of a subset of yeast proteins is likely triggered by a more oxidizing redox environment, which causes those protein thiols that can undergo stabilizing disulfide bonds with nearby cysteines to accumulate in their oxidized state.
source: These results suggest that the early oxidation of a subset of yeast proteins is likely triggered by a more oxidizing redox environment, which causes those protein thiols that can undergo stabilizing disulfide bonds with nearby cysteines to accumulate in their oxidized state.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early-oxidized proteins have nearby cysteines that can form disulfide bonds.

claim: A sudden surge in ROS, such as peroxide, causing oxidation of particularly ROS-sensitive proteins appears less likely as only a few previously identified peroxide-sensitive cysteines and none of the most peroxide-sensitive peptides were found among the group of early oxidation targets.
source: One alternative explanation, that a sudden surge in ROS, such as peroxide, causes oxidation of a group of particularly ROS-sensitive proteins, appears less likely as only a few of our previously identified peroxide-sensitive cysteines and none of our most peroxide-sensitive peptides (i.e., GapDH) were found among the group of early oxidation targets (Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of early oxidation targets shown in Table 1.

claim: At least 28 proteins showed oxidation that significantly preceded the general oxidation of proteins under standard or caloric restriction conditions.
source: Oxidation of at least 28 proteins significantly preceded the general oxidation of proteins under standard or caloric restriction conditions (Figure 3, clusters D and E and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Of the early-oxidized proteins, 20 had oxidation states of more than 45% at day 2 of cultivation, which was 1.5- to 3.8-fold higher than their oxidation status during exponential growth.
source: Of these early-oxidized proteins, 20 had oxidation states of more than 45% at day 2 of cultivation, which was 1.5- to 3.8-fold higher than their oxidation status during exponential growth.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Table 1.

claim: Thioredoxin reductase is the key component of the thioredoxin system.
source: One of these early oxidation targets is the highly conserved enzyme thioredoxin reductase, the key component of the thioredoxin system.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the thioredoxin system.

claim: Loss of thioredoxin reductase activity has been shown to cause widespread protein oxidation.
source: Loss of thioredoxin reductase activity has been shown to cause widespread protein oxidation (Holmgren and Lu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Holmgren and Lu, 2010.

claim: The oxidation of thioredoxin reductase's two active site cysteines raised sharply by about twofold to 65% at least 24 hr before the general redox collapse began.
source: We found that the oxidation of thioredoxin reductase's two active site cysteines, which are arranged in the prototypical C-X-X-C motif, raised sharply by about twofold to 65% at least 24 hr before the general redox collapse began (Figure 5, compare blue and red trace)
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Thioredoxin reductase oxidation was close to 80% at day 3 of cultivation under standard conditions.
source: and was close to 80% at day 3 of cultivation under standard conditions (Figure 5 and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Under caloric restriction, oxidation of thioredoxin reductase was delayed by 48 hr relative to standard conditions but again preceded the general redox collapse by about 24 hr.
source: The same trend was observed under caloric restriction: although oxidation of thioredoxin reductase was delayed by 48 hr relative to what was seen under standard conditions, it again preceded the general redox collapse by about 24 hr (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Table 1.

claim: A shift to extreme caloric restriction (water) partially reversed the early oxidation of thioredoxin reductase that was noticeable at day 2 of cultivation.
source: Note that a shift to extreme caloric restriction (water) partially reversed the early oxidation of thioredoxin reductase that was noticeable at day 2 of cultivation (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Within 24 hr upon shift into water, a significant reduction in thioredoxin reductase's oxidation status was observed, which reached levels only slightly above the initial oxidation levels in exponentially growing yeast cells.
source: Within 24 hr upon shift into water, we observed a significant reduction in thioredoxin reductase's oxidation status, which reached levels that were only slightly above the initial oxidation levels of thioredoxin reductase in exponentially growing yeast cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Early interventions restore the activity of thioredoxin reductase and prevent the collapse of cellular redox homeostasis.
source: These results suggest that early interventions restore the activity of thioredoxin reductase and also prevent the collapse of cellular redox homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that shifting to water reverses thioredoxin reductase oxidation and prevents general protein oxidation.

claim: Δtrr2 mutants grew like wild-type yeast cells and had a wild-type like chronological lifespan.
source: We found that while Δtrr2 mutants grew like wild-type yeast cells and had a wild-type like chronological lifespan
evidence: This claim is based on lifespan measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the cytosolic TRR1 homologue (Δtrr1) caused severe growth defects and a significantly shortened lifespan.
source: deletion of the cytosolic TRR1 homologue (Δtrr1) caused severe growth defects and a significantly shortened lifespan (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on lifespan measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Healthy-looking Δtrr1 suppressors were generated with very high frequency.
source: Moreover, we observed the generation of healthy-looking Δtrr1 suppressors with very high frequency.
evidence: This is an observation made during the study.

claim: Cultivation of Δtrr1 deletion mutants without the potential generation of suppressors was only possible when the medium was supplemented with cysteine.
source: In fact, cultivation of Δtrr1 deletion mutants without the potential generation of suppressors was only possible when the medium was supplemented with cysteine, presumably to maintain proteins in their reduced state.
evidence: This is an observation made during the study.

claim: Organisms lacking thioredoxin reductase have previously been shown to be either severely compromised in growth or non-viable.
source: Organisms lacking thioredoxin reductase have previously been shown to be either severely compromised in growth or non-viable (Holmgren and Lu, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Holmgren and Lu, 2010.

claim: The NADPH-dependent thioredoxin system is one of two highly conserved multi-enzyme systems that contribute to the maintenance of cellular redox homeostasis in most pro- and eukaryotic organisms.
source: The NADPH-dependent thioredoxin system is one of two highly conserved multi-enzyme systems that contribute to the maintenance of cellular redox homeostasis in most pro- and eukaryotic organisms.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cellular redox systems.

claim: The other redox system consists of NADPH-dependent glutathione reductase, several small glutaredoxins, and the cysteine-containing tripeptide glutathione (GSH), which together with its oxidized counterpart GSSG determines the cellular redox potential.
source: The other system consists of NADPH-dependent glutathione reductase, several small glutaredoxins, and the cysteine-containing tripeptide glutathione (GSH), which together with its oxidized counterpart GSSG determines the cellular redox potential (Martensson and Meister, 1989; Merad-Boudia et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martensson and Meister, 1989 and Merad-Boudia et al., 1998.

claim: During exponential growth, the glutathione redox potential did not differ between yeast cells cultivated in standard or caloric restriction conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, we found that during exponential growth, the glutathione redox potential did not differ between yeast cells cultivated in standard or caloric restriction conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: By day 1 of cultivation in standard conditions, yeast cells showed an at least 15 mV increase in their overall redox potential.
source: However, by day 1 of cultivation in standard conditions, yeast cells showed an at least 15 mV increase in their overall redox potential, which induces a significant shift in the thiol/disulfide or thiol/sulfenic acid equilibrium of proteins that are in equilibrium with the GSH/GSSG couple.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Yeast cells cultivated under caloric restriction conditions experienced a much smaller initial increase in the cellular redox potential.
source: In contrast, yeast cells cultivated under caloric restriction conditions experienced a much smaller initial increase in the cellular redox potential.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cells cultivated in caloric restriction media showed a 48-hr delay to reach the same redox potential observed in cells cultivated in standard media.
source: Importantly, cells cultivated in caloric restriction media showed a 48-hr delay to reach the same redox potential observed in cells cultivated in standard media (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The 48-hr delay in redox potential change under caloric restriction is consistent with the previously observed 48-hr delay in protein oxidation.
source: This delay is consistent with our previously observed 48-hr delay in protein oxidation in yeast cells cultivated in caloric restriction media as opposed to standard media.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the redox potential measurements with the protein oxidation data.

claim: Both thioredoxin reductase and glutathione reductase draw their reducing power from NADPH, making the oxidation status of these systems ultimately dependent on cellular NADPH and NADP+ levels.
source: Both thioredoxin reductase and glutathione reductase draw their reducing power from NADPH, making the oxidation status of these systems ultimately dependent on cellular NADPH and NADP+ levels.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the biochemistry of these enzyme systems.

claim: Exponentially growing yeast cells have very similar levels of NADPH and NADP+ independent of their initial glucose availability.
source: We found that exponentially growing yeast cells have very similar levels of NADPH and NADP+ independent of their initial glucose availability, and that these levels increased over the next 12 hr under both cultivation conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NADPH and NADP+ levels increased over the 12 hours following exponential growth under both cultivation conditions.
source: We found that exponentially growing yeast cells have very similar levels of NADPH and NADP+ independent of their initial glucose availability, and that these levels increased over the next 12 hr under both cultivation conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Yeast cells undergo a diauxic shift from glucose-driven fermentation to ethanol-driven respiration during the time frame when NADPH levels increase.
source: In this time frame, yeast cells undergo a diauxic shift from glucose-driven fermentation to ethanol-driven respiration.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about yeast metabolism.

claim: Cells induce NADH kinases such as UTR1 and POS5, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (ZWF1), and the cytosolic NADPH-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (Idp2) to increase NADPH production and regeneration.
source: Cells induce NADH kinases such as UTR1 and POS5, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (ZWF1), and the cytosolic NADPH-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (Idp2) to increase NADPH production and regeneration (Gasch et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gasch et al., 2000.

claim: In cells cultivated under standard conditions, the intracellular levels of NADPH rapidly decreased over the 24-hr time period following the initial increase.
source: In cells cultivated under standard conditions, the intracellular levels of NADPH then rapidly decreased over the next 24-hr time period.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In cells cultivated under caloric restriction conditions, NADPH levels decreased with much slower rates and reached concentrations comparable to those observed in standard media with about a 48-hr delay.
source: In contrast, in cells cultivated under caloric restriction conditions, NADPH levels decreased with much slower rates and reached concentrations comparable to those observed in standard media with about a 48-hr delay (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The drop in intracellular NADPH levels coincided well with the initial oxidation of thioredoxin reductase and the alteration in the cellular redox potential.
source: This drop in intracellular NADPH levels coincided well with the initial oxidation of thioredoxin reductase and the alteration in the cellular redox potential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation of NADPH decrease, thioredoxin reductase oxidation, and redox potential changes.

claim: Early changes in cellular NADPH levels might serve as trigger for the initial oxidation of thioredoxin reductase and changes in the cellular redox potential, which subsequently leads to the redox collapse observed in postmitotic yeast cells.
source: In summary, these results suggest that early changes in cellular NADPH levels might serve as trigger for the initial oxidation of thioredoxin reductase and changes in the cellular redox potential, which subsequently leads to the redox collapse observed in postmitotic yeast cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation of NADPH decrease with protein oxidation events.

claim: Cultivation under caloric restriction conditions appears to delay the decrease in cellular NADPH levels, delays the redox collapse of the yeast proteome, and extends lifespan.
source: Cultivation under caloric restriction conditions appears to delay the decrease in cellular NADPH levels, delays the redox collapse of the yeast proteome, and extends lifespan.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing delayed NADPH decrease, delayed protein oxidation, and extended lifespan under caloric restriction.

claim: Early during the chronological aging process and significantly before cell death sets in, yeast cells undergo an abrupt loss in redox homeostasis as indicated by the massive oxidation of the large majority of thiol-containing cytosolic, nuclear, and mitochondrial proteins.
source: We made the very surprising observation that early during the chronological aging process and significantly before cell death sets in, yeast cells undergo an abrupt loss in redox homeostasis as indicated by the massive oxidation of the large majority of thiol-containing cytosolic, nuclear, and mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This is based on the OxICAT data showing widespread protein oxidation days before cell death.

claim: The oxidation event is significantly delayed by caloric restriction and even more so by a shift to hypometabolic cultivation conditions.
source: Importantly, this oxidation event is significantly delayed by caloric restriction and even more so by a shift to hypometabolic cultivation conditions
evidence: This is based on the OxICAT data comparing different cultivation conditions.

claim: Maintenance of redox homeostasis might contribute to the lifespan extending effects of caloric restriction and hypometabolic cultivation.
source: suggesting that maintenance of redox homeostasis might contribute to the lifespan extending effects of these regimens.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between delayed oxidation and extended lifespan under caloric restriction.

claim: Thiol oxidation occurs in at least two waves.
source: We noted that thiol oxidation occurs in at least two waves.
evidence: This is based on cluster analysis showing early oxidation targets (clusters D and E) and general oxidation targets (clusters A-C).

claim: The first wave of oxidation affects only a very small subset of identified thiol-containing proteins (<10%) and hit cells cultivated in standard media within 24–48 hr after reaching exponential growth.
source: The first wave, which affects only a very small subset of identified thiol-containing proteins (<10%), hit cells cultivated in standard media within 24–48 hr after reaching exponential growth.
evidence: This is based on cluster analysis showing that about 10% of proteins are in clusters D and E.

claim: At the time of the first wave of oxidation, cells had stopped dividing, transitioned to respiratory growth, and NADPH levels had started to decrease significantly.
source: At this point, cells had stopped dividing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), transitioned to respiratory growth, and NADPH levels, which transiently increased during the diauxic shift, had started to decrease significantly (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on growth data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and NADPH measurements (Figure 6B).

claim: The second wave of oxidation occurred about 24 hr after the first wave and affected nearly 70% of the remaining identified yeast protein thiols.
source: The second wave of oxidation, which occurred about 24 hr later, affected nearly 70% of the remaining identified yeast protein thiols (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Yeast cells were able to maintain their energy resources (i.e., ATP levels) and to survive for several more days after the collapse.
source: Yet as observed before, yeast cells were able to maintain their energy resources (i.e., ATP levels) and to survive for several more days after the collapse.
evidence: This is based on ATP measurements (Figure 2B) and viability data (Figure 1A).

claim: Many of the very early oxidation targets are cysteines that form part of a C-X2/3-C motif.
source: Bioinformatic analysis revealed that many of the very early oxidation targets are cysteines that form part of a C-X2/3-C motif (e.g., thioredoxin reductase, CCT4, CCT8, YdJ1, RPL42, PAA1, MES1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of early oxidation targets.

claim: The C-X2/3-C cysteine motif is often found in disulfide oxidoreductases, redox-sensitive transcription factors, and many metal binding proteins, and confers considerable redox sensitivity to proteins.
source: This cysteine motif is often found in disulfide oxidoreductases, redox-sensitive transcription factors, and many metal binding proteins, and confers considerable redox sensitivity to proteins (Sanchez et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sanchez et al., 2008.

claim: The C-X2/3-C cysteine motif allows many proteins to form transient disulfide bonds within the otherwise reducing environment of the cytosol.
source: Hence, this cysteine motif allows many of these proteins to form transient disulfide bonds within the otherwise reducing environment of the cytosol.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the properties of the C-X2/3-C motif.

claim: Only 5 of the 28 early oxidation targets were previously identified to contain peroxide-sensitive thiols.
source: However, we found that only 5 of the 28 early oxidation targets were previously identified to contain peroxide-sensitive thiols (Table 1, indicated with asterisk).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous studies and data shown in Table 1.

claim: Protein thiols that were previously identified to be highly peroxide-sensitive, such as the active site cysteines of GapDH or AHP1, were not among the early oxidation targets in yeast.
source: Moreover, protein thiols that we had previously identified to be highly peroxide-sensitive, such as the active site cysteines of GapDH or AHP1 (a thiol-peroxidase that undergoes reversible disulfide bond formation upon peroxide detoxification) were not among the early oxidation targets in yeast (Figure 1—Source data 1).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1—Source data 1.

claim: Elevated peroxide production is unlikely the cause of the early oxidation event.
source: These results suggested that elevated peroxide production is unlikely the cause of the early oxidation event.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that peroxide-sensitive proteins are not among early oxidation targets.

claim: The early oxidation event is significantly preceded by a loss in cellular NADPH, the electron donor of the NADPH-dependent thioredoxin system.
source: Instead, we noted that the early oxidation event is significantly preceded by a loss in cellular NADPH, the electron donor of the NADPH-dependent thioredoxin system.
evidence: This is based on the temporal correlation between NADPH decrease and protein oxidation.

claim: Under conditions of caloric restriction, each of the individual processes (NADPH decrease, early protein oxidation, and the collapse of the thiol redox proteome) was time-delayed by about 48 hr.
source: Moreover, we found that under conditions of caloric restriction, each of the individual processes was time-delayed by about 48 hr: NADPH decrease, early protein (i.e., thioredoxin reductase) oxidation, and the collapse of the thiol redox proteome.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from standard and caloric restriction conditions.

claim: Loss of NADPH might be the trigger for the observed redox collapse.
source: These findings raised the intriguing possibility that these processes are directly connected (Figure 7) and that loss of NADPH might be the trigger for the observed redox collapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation and the known role of NADPH in maintaining redox homeostasis.

claim: Analysis of the cellular GSH/GSSG ratio in chronologically aging yeast cells revealed a pro-oxidizing shift in the GSH redox potential that coincided with the decrease in cellular NADPH levels.
source: Consistent with this idea, analysis of the cellular GSH/GSSG ratio in chronologically aging yeast cells, which is dependent on the NADPH-dependent glutathione reductase, revealed a pro-oxidizing shift in the GSH redox potential that coincided with the decrease in cellular NADPH levels.
evidence: This is based on GSH/GSSG measurements (Figure 6A) and NADPH measurements (Figure 6B).

claim: The pro-oxidizing shift in GSH redox potential was significantly delayed in calorically restricted growth conditions.
source: As before, this pro-oxidizing shift was significantly delayed in calorically restricted growth conditions (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A reduction in caloric intake transiently increases cellular NADPH levels, which is able to extend maintenance of the cellular redox balance and might contribute to lifespan extension.
source: These findings would explain how a reduction in caloric intake, which transiently increases cellular NADPH levels (Figure 6B), is able to extend maintenance of the cellular redox balance and might contribute to lifespan extension.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between increased NADPH levels, delayed oxidation, and extended lifespan under caloric restriction.

claim: Similar pro-oxidizing shifts in thioredoxin and glutathione systems have been observed in aging rodents.
source: It is noteworthy that similar pro-oxidizing shifts in thioredoxin and glutathione systems have also been observed in aging rodents (Cho et al., 2003; Rohrbach et al., 2006; Rebrin and Sohal, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2003; Rohrbach et al., 2006; and Rebrin and Sohal, 2008.

claim: Pro-oxidizing shifts in redox systems in aging rodents might, at least in part, be explained by the observed decrease in cellular NADPH levels in aging rats.
source: and might, at least in part, be explained by the observed decrease in cellular NADPH levels in aging rats (Parihar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parihar et al., 2008.

claim: Caloric restriction at least partially reversed the detected changes in redox status in rodents, shifted the glutathione pool to a more reducing redox potential relative to cultures grown in 2% glucose, and increased cellular NADPH levels.
source: Consistent with our studies, caloric restriction at least partially reversed the detected changes in redox status, shifted the glutathione pool to a more reducing redox potential relative to cultures grown in 2% glucose, and increased cellular NADPH levels (Someya et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Someya et al., 2010.

claim: The observed decrease in cellular NADPH levels and the concomitant increase in cellular redox potential is not just a yeast-specific event but might be shared with other aging organisms as their metabolism changes.
source: These results suggest that the observed decrease in cellular NADPH levels and the concomitant increase in cellular redox potential is not just a yeast-specific event but might be shared with other aging organisms as their metabolism changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with studies in rodents.

claim: Yeast cells undergo the very same pattern of NADPH decrease, Trr1 oxidation and redox collapse (albeit time-delayed) when cultivated in 2% glucose or in 0.5% glucose medium.
source: The fact that yeast cells undergo the very same pattern of NADPH decrease, Trr1 oxidation and redox collapse (albeit time-delayed) when cultivated in 2% glucose or in 0.5% glucose medium also argues against the possibility that medium acidification, which has been discussed to accelerate chronological aging in yeast, is a contributing factor to the observed effects
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from standard and caloric restriction conditions.

claim: Medium acidification is not a contributing factor to the observed effects, as medium acidification is severe in 2% glucose yet insignificant in 0.5% glucose.
source: as medium acidification is severe in 2% glucose yet insignificant in 0.5% glucose (Burtner et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burtner et al., 2009.

claim: Early protein oxidation is, at least in its initial stage, a fully reversible event in yeast.
source: It was intriguing to observe that early protein oxidation is, at least in its initial stage, a fully reversible event in yeast.
evidence: This is based on the observation that shifting cells to water reverses thioredoxin reductase oxidation (Figure 5).

claim: More than 80% of viable cells were recovered from day 3- and day 4-old cultures despite an almost fully oxidized thiol proteome.
source: Moreover, we found that more than 80% of viable cells were recovered from day 3- and day 4-old cultures despite an almost fully oxidized thiol proteome.
evidence: This is based on viability measurements (Figure 1A) and oxidation data (Figure 2A).

claim: Oxidative thiol modifications might serve a beneficial purpose for cells by preventing irreversible thiol modifications that would ultimately lead to protein degradation and potentially cell death.
source: It has been suggested that oxidative thiol modifications, such as those detected by our OxICAT method, might serve a beneficial purpose for cells by preventing irreversible thiol modifications that would ultimately lead to protein degradation and potentially cell death (Gallogly and Mieyal, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gallogly and Mieyal, 2007.

claim: The initially reversible thiol modifications observed in chronologically aging yeast cells might represent a 'pro-active' response to protect proteins against irreversible protein modifications and damage, and thereby extend lifespan.
source: It is thus tempting to speculate that the initially reversible thiol modifications that we observe in chronologically aging yeast cells might in fact represent a 'pro-active' response of yeast cells to protect their proteins against irreversible protein modifications and damage, and thereby extend lifespan.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of reversible oxidation and cell survival.

claim: Quantitative studies in diamide-treated HeLa and HEK cells revealed that over 50% of protein thiols undergo reversible thiol modifications in response to diamide stress.
source: Quantitative studies conducted in diamide-treated HeLa and HEK cells revealed that over 50% of protein thiols undergo reversible thiol modifications in response to diamide stress, providing evidence that the combined redox proteome of mammalian cells has a higher redox buffering capacity than glutathione (Hansen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2009.

claim: The combined redox proteome of mammalian cells has a higher redox buffering capacity than glutathione.
source: Quantitative studies conducted in diamide-treated HeLa and HEK cells revealed that over 50% of protein thiols undergo reversible thiol modifications in response to diamide stress, providing evidence that the combined redox proteome of mammalian cells has a higher redox buffering capacity than glutathione (Hansen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2009.

claim: The majority of yeast protein thiols have the capacity to undergo reversible redox modifications and thereby serve as redox buffer.
source: While the authors were unable to conclude whether this high redox buffering capacity of protein thiols is the work of a few high abundance, highly cysteine-enriched proteins or a contribution of the majority of thiol-containing proteins, our data suggest that the majority of yeast protein thiols have the capacity to undergo reversible redox modifications and thereby serve as redox buffer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that over 80% of protein thiols become oxidized.

claim: Chronological aging might represent a physiological stress condition that utilizes and stresses the redox buffering capacity of the thiol proteome.
source: These results suggest that chronological aging might represent a physiological stress condition that utilizes and stresses the redox buffering capacity of the thiol proteome.
evidence: This is speculation based on the widespread protein oxidation observed during aging.

claim: Oxidation of some key proteins might contribute to the potentially beneficial down-regulation of cellular processes that would otherwise negatively affect yeast lifespan.
source: At this point, we also cannot exclude that oxidation of some key proteins might actually contribute to the potentially beneficial down-regulation of cellular processes that would otherwise negatively affect yeast lifespan and shorten it even more.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential adaptive role of protein oxidation.

claim: Methionyl-tRNA synthetase (MES1) is an enzyme involved in translational initiation.
source: One such example would be methionyl-tRNA synthetase (MES1), an enzyme involved in translational initiation (Delarue, 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delarue, 1995.

claim: Oxidation of Cys353 in MES1 reaches over 65% at day 2 of cultivation in standard conditions.
source: whose oxidation of Cys353 reaches over 65% at day 2 of cultivation in standard conditions (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Table 1.

claim: Cys353 in MES1 is part of a zinc finger-like CX2C-X9-CX2C motif whose substitution in the E. coli homologue MetRS causes a strong decrease in enzyme activity.
source: Intriguingly, Cys353 is part of a zinc finger-like CX2C-X9-CX2C motif whose substitution in the E. coli homologue MetRS causes a strong decrease in enzyme activity (Fourmy et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fourmy et al., 1993.

claim: Down-regulation of protein translation has been shown to contribute to increased oxidative stress resistance and to extend lifespan in replicative aging yeast and other organisms.
source: Down-regulation of protein translation has been shown to contribute to increased oxidative stress resistance and to extend lifespan in replicative aging yeast and other organisms (Steffen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Steffen et al., 2008.
